title: Protecting Angular routes with route guards
description: Use functional guards for navigation while keeping the server as the authorization boundary.
content:
## Functional guards

Angular functional guards can decide whether navigation may continue, redirect to another route, or wait for an asynchronous result. They are useful for checking session state and improving the navigation experience.

## Handle permissions clearly

A guard can read route metadata to determine which permission is needed and return a UrlTree when the current user should be redirected. Prefer a single, consistent authorization helper over duplicating permission checks across routes.

## Protect APIs too

A route guard runs in the browser and can be bypassed by a user who controls that browser. Every protected backend endpoint must independently authenticate the request and verify permissions before returning or changing data.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Using IAM roles instead of long-lived AWS access keys
description: Give applications temporary credentials through IAM roles and reduce key-management risk.
content:
## Prefer temporary credentials

Applications running on AWS can obtain temporary credentials through an attached IAM role rather than storing long-lived access keys. The AWS SDK credential provider chain can retrieve and refresh these credentials automatically in supported environments.

## Apply least privilege

Attach policies that grant only the actions and resources the workload needs. Use separate roles for different applications or environments, and avoid sharing a powerful role across unrelated systems.

## Review identity access

Audit role trust policies, permissions, and usage. Never commit access keys to source control or bake them into container images; rotate and revoke any exposed credentials promptly.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Building reliable quality gates in a CI pipeline
description: Use repeatable builds, automated checks, and clear release evidence to reduce deployment risk.
content:
## Validate every change

A useful CI pipeline checks out a specific revision, restores dependencies reproducibly, compiles the application, and runs appropriate tests and static checks. Failures should be visible and tied to the change that introduced them.

## Promote one artifact

Build an immutable artifact once and promote that same artifact through environments. Rebuilding separately for production can produce different outputs and makes release verification less reliable.

## Keep secrets and approvals safe

Provide credentials through the CI platform's protected secret mechanism, scope them to the smallest required job, and avoid printing them. Add human approval where policy or risk requires it, and keep a rollback path for failed releases.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Docker container networking fundamentals
description: Connect containers with Docker networks and understand service-name discovery.
content:
## User-defined bridge networks

Containers attached to the same user-defined bridge network can communicate using their container or service names. Docker provides DNS-based discovery on these networks, which is generally more reliable than hard-coding container IP addresses.

## Publish ports deliberately

A container port is not automatically exposed to the host. Publish only the ports that need to be reachable from outside the Docker network, and bind to a specific host interface when broad exposure is not desired.

## Keep network boundaries clear

Separate unrelated services into appropriate networks and avoid assuming that a published port is private. Review firewall rules and the application's own authentication and authorization independently of Docker networking.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Deploying a stateless service to Google Cloud Run
description: Package an HTTP service in a container and configure Cloud Run for scalable requests.
content:
## Prepare the service

Cloud Run runs a container that serves HTTP requests and listens on the port provided by the runtime environment. Build a reproducible image, keep the process in the foreground, and handle termination signals so the service can shut down cleanly.

## Design for stateless instances

Instances can scale out or stop at any time. Store durable state in managed storage rather than the container's local filesystem, and make request handling safe when traffic reaches different instances.

## Configure access and scaling

Choose whether the service is public or requires authentication, grant the runtime service account only the permissions it needs, and set concurrency and scaling limits based on load tests and downstream capacity.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Understanding the Hibernate entity lifecycle
description: Learn the transient, managed, detached, and removed entity states.
content:
## Entity states

A transient entity is a newly created Java object not associated with a persistence context. A managed entity is tracked by an EntityManager or Session, and changes can be synchronized during flush. A detached entity has an identity but is no longer tracked by that context. A removed entity is scheduled for deletion.

## Dirty checking

Hibernate detects changes to managed entities and can generate SQL during flush without an explicit update call. This behavior applies only while the entity is managed and within the persistence context.

## Work with detached data carefully

When updating from an API request, avoid blindly merging client-supplied entities. Load the managed entity, validate the requested changes, and update allowed fields to avoid overwriting data the client should not control.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Avoiding the N+1 Query Problem in Hibernate
description: Learn how N+1 issues occur and techniques to optimize data fetching.
content:
## What is N+1?

The N+1 problem occurs when Hibernate executes one query to fetch parent entities and additional queries for each associated entity.

## Common causes

Improper lazy loading and frequent access to child collections inside loops often create N+1 performance issues.

## Interview checkpoint

Discuss JOIN FETCH, EntityGraph, batch fetching, lazy loading, and eager loading strategies.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Java Collections: choosing the right collection
description: Understand the core collection interfaces and select the right data structure for common interview problems.
content:
## The collection hierarchy

The Java Collections Framework provides interfaces such as List, Set, Queue, and Map. List preserves order and allows duplicates. Set enforces uniqueness. Queue models processing order, while Map associates keys with values.

## Choosing a collection

Use ArrayList for indexed access and iteration. LinkedList can be useful for frequent operations at both ends, but ArrayDeque is usually a better queue or stack. HashSet and HashMap provide average constant-time lookup when hashCode and equals are implemented consistently. Choose TreeSet or TreeMap when sorted order is required.

## Interview checkpoint

Explain the ordering, uniqueness, and lookup requirements before selecting a collection. Include expected time complexity and any thread-safety requirements in your answer.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: How to Synchronize ArrayList?
content: ArrayList is not synchronized by default. It can be synchronized using Collections.synchronizedList(list) or by using CopyOnWriteArrayList. These approaches make ArrayList safe for use in multi-threaded applications.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: When to Use ArrayList and LinkedList?
content: Use ArrayList when frequent search and read operations are required. Use LinkedList when insertion and deletion operations occur frequently. ArrayList provides faster random access whereas LinkedList provides faster updates.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Ways to Traverse Collection Elements
content: Collections can be traversed using Iterator, ListIterator, enhanced for-loop, traditional for-loop, forEach() method, and forEachRemaining() method. Each technique is suited for different requirements.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: What is forEach() Method?
content: forEach() was introduced in Java 8 and uses lambda expressions to iterate through elements. It provides a concise and readable way to process collection elements.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: What is forEachRemaining() Method?
content: forEachRemaining() is available on Iterator and processes all remaining elements using a Consumer implementation. It simplifies iteration using lambda expressions.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: How to Compare Two ArrayLists?
content: Two ArrayLists can be compared using equals(), removeAll(), retainAll(), contains(), Streams API, and contentEquals(). The choice depends on whether you need exact matching or common elements.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: What is retainAll() Method?
content: retainAll() retains only the elements present in both collections. It is commonly used to find intersection/common values between lists or sets.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: What is removeAll() Method?
content: removeAll() removes all elements that exist in another collection. It is useful for finding the differences between collections.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: What is contains() Method?
content: contains() checks whether a collection contains a specified element. It internally uses equals() to perform comparisons.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: What is Collections.sort()?
content: Collections.sort() sorts List elements in ascending order. Elements must implement Comparable or a Comparator must be supplied.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Explain List Interface
content: List interface is the child interface of Collection interface. It maintains insertion order and allows duplicate elements. Elements can be accessed using indexes. The main implementations are ArrayList, LinkedList, Vector, and Stack.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Explain ArrayList
content: ArrayList is a resizable implementation of the List interface. It uses a dynamic array internally, maintains insertion order, allows duplicates and null values, and provides fast random access. Default capacity is 10.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Explain LinkedList
content: LinkedList uses a doubly linked list data structure. It implements both List and Deque interfaces. It maintains insertion order, allows duplicates, and provides efficient insertion and deletion operations.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Explain ConcurrentHashMap
content: ConcurrentHashMap is a thread-safe implementation of Map introduced in Java 5. It allows concurrent read and write operations without locking the entire map. It provides better performance than Hashtable in multi-threaded environments and does not allow null keys or null values.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Difference Between HashMap and ConcurrentHashMap
content: HashMap is not thread-safe while ConcurrentHashMap is thread-safe. HashMap allows one null key and multiple null values; ConcurrentHashMap does not allow null keys or values. HashMap throws ConcurrentModificationException during concurrent modification whereas ConcurrentHashMap does not.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: ConcurrentHashMap vs SynchronizedMap
content: ConcurrentHashMap uses segment/bucket-level locking and supports concurrent reads and writes. SynchronizedMap locks the entire map during operations. ConcurrentHashMap provides better scalability and performance in multi-threaded applications.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Explain Vector
content: Vector is a legacy class that implements List interface. It uses a dynamic array internally and is synchronized. It is thread-safe but slower than ArrayList because every method is synchronized.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Explain Stack
content: Stack extends Vector and follows Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) principle. Important methods include push(), pop(), peek(), empty(), and search().
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Explain Queue Interface
content: Queue represents a FIFO data structure. Elements are inserted at the rear and removed from the front. Common implementations include PriorityQueue, LinkedList, ArrayDeque, and BlockingQueue.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Explain PriorityQueue
content: PriorityQueue stores elements according to their priority rather than insertion order. It does not allow null values and uses a heap data structure internally.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Explain Deque Interface
content: Deque stands for Double Ended Queue. It allows insertion and deletion from both ends. It can work as both a Queue (FIFO) and a Stack (LIFO).
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Explain ArrayDeque
content: ArrayDeque implements Deque and uses a resizable array internally. It does not allow null values and is faster than Stack and LinkedList for stack and queue operations.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Explain Set Interface
content: Set represents a collection of unique elements. It does not allow duplicates. Implementations include HashSet, LinkedHashSet, and TreeSet.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Explain HashSet
content: HashSet implements Set interface and uses HashMap internally. It stores unique elements, does not maintain insertion order, allows one null value, and provides fast search operations.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Explain LinkedHashSet
content: LinkedHashSet extends HashSet and maintains insertion order. It provides unique elements like HashSet while preserving the order in which elements were inserted.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Explain SortedSet
content: SortedSet is an alternative to Set that maintains elements in sorted order. Elements are arranged according to their natural ordering or a Comparator.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Explain TreeSet
content: TreeSet implements NavigableSet and SortedSet. It stores unique elements in ascending order, does not allow null values, and uses TreeMap internally.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Explain EnumSet
content: EnumSet is a specialized Set implementation designed specifically for enum types. It provides high performance and type safety when working with enum constants.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Explain Map Interface
content: Map stores data as key-value pairs. Keys must be unique while values can be duplicated. Map does not extend Collection interface. Common implementations are HashMap, LinkedHashMap, TreeMap, and Hashtable.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Explain HashMap
content: HashMap stores key-value pairs using hashing. It allows one null key and multiple null values. It is non-synchronized and provides average O(1) insertion and retrieval time.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Explain LinkedHashMap
content: LinkedHashMap extends HashMap and maintains insertion order. It combines the performance benefits of HashMap with predictable iteration order.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Explain TreeMap
content: TreeMap implements SortedMap and NavigableMap. It stores entries in ascending order of keys using a Red-Black Tree. Null keys are not allowed.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Explain Hashtable
content: Hashtable is a legacy synchronized implementation of Map. It does not allow null keys or values. Because of synchronization overhead, it is slower than HashMap.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: What is Collection Framework in Java?
content: Collection Framework is a combination of classes and interfaces used to store and manipulate data in the form of objects. It provides ready-to-use data structures such as ArrayList, LinkedList, Vector, Stack, HashSet, TreeSet, HashMap, and Hashtable. The framework offers reusable architecture for storing, retrieving, sorting, and manipulating data efficiently.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: What is the difference between Array and Collection?
content: Arrays are fixed in size while collections are dynamically resizable. Arrays can store only homogeneous elements whereas collections can store heterogeneous objects. Arrays do not provide built-in methods for searching and sorting, while collections provide ready-made utility methods through Collections class.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Explain Collection Framework Interfaces
content: The major interfaces are Collection, List, Set, Queue, Deque, and Map. List maintains order and duplicates. Set stores unique elements. Queue follows FIFO. Deque supports insertion and deletion from both ends. Map stores key-value pairs.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: What are Legacy Classes in Collection Framework?
content: Legacy classes are classes introduced before Collection Framework in JDK 1.2. Examples include Vector, Stack, Hashtable, Dictionary, and Properties. Most of these classes are synchronized and considered legacy implementations.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: What is Enumeration Interface?
content: Enumeration is a legacy cursor used to traverse legacy collections such as Vector and Hashtable. It supports only reading elements. It does not support element removal and is not fail-fast.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Difference Between ArrayList and Vector
content: ArrayList is non-synchronized and not thread-safe. Vector is synchronized and thread-safe. ArrayList grows by 50% when capacity is exceeded, whereas Vector doubles its capacity. ArrayList provides better performance than Vector because it avoids synchronization overhead.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Difference Between ArrayList and LinkedList
content: ArrayList uses a dynamic array internally and provides fast random access. LinkedList uses a doubly linked list and offers faster insertions and deletions. ArrayList consumes less memory, while LinkedList requires additional memory for node references.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Difference Between Iterator and ListIterator
content: Iterator supports forward traversal only and can remove elements. ListIterator supports both forward and backward traversal and can perform add(), set(), and remove() operations while iterating.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Difference Between Iterator and Enumeration
content: Iterator works with both legacy and modern collections and supports remove operation. Enumeration works only with legacy collections and supports traversal only. Iterator is fail-fast while Enumeration is not fail-fast.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Difference Between List and Set
content: List maintains insertion order and allows duplicate elements. Set does not allow duplicate elements. List can contain multiple null values whereas Set typically allows only one null value.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Difference Between HashSet and TreeSet
content: HashSet stores elements using hashing and does not maintain order. TreeSet stores elements in sorted ascending order using a tree structure. HashSet provides better performance for search operations compared to TreeSet.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Difference Between Set and Map
content: Set stores only values and enforces uniqueness. Map stores key-value pairs. A Map contains unique keys but may contain duplicate values.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Difference Between HashSet and HashMap
content: HashSet stores unique objects only and internally uses HashMap. HashMap stores key-value pairs. HashSet uses object as key internally and a dummy object as value.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Difference Between HashMap and TreeMap
content: HashMap stores entries without maintaining order. TreeMap stores entries in ascending order of keys. HashMap uses hashing whereas TreeMap uses Red-Black Tree implementation.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Difference Between HashMap and Hashtable
content: HashMap is non-synchronized and allows one null key and multiple null values. Hashtable is synchronized and does not allow null keys or values. HashMap is faster whereas Hashtable is slower due to synchronization overhead.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Difference Between Collection and Collections
content: Collection is an interface representing a group of objects. Collections is a utility class that provides static methods such as sort(), reverse(), binarySearch(), synchronizedList(), and unmodifiableList().
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Difference Between Comparable and Comparator
content: Comparable provides a single natural sorting order through compareTo(). Comparator provides multiple sorting strategies through compare(). Comparable belongs to java.lang package, while Comparator belongs to java.util package.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: How HashMap Works Internally?
content: HashMap works on the principle of hashing. When a key-value pair is inserted, hashCode() determines the bucket location. If multiple keys produce the same bucket, collision handling occurs using linked lists or balanced trees. equals() is used to identify the correct key.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: What is Hashing?
content: Hashing is the process of converting an object into a fixed numeric value called hash code using hashCode() method. Equal objects must produce the same hash code. Hashing is used to store and retrieve objects efficiently in HashMap, HashSet, and Hashtable.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: What is Entry Class in HashMap?
content: HashMap internally stores data in Entry objects. An Entry contains key, value, hash, and reference to the next Entry. Entries form linked structures inside buckets to handle collisions. Each bucket can contain one or multiple Entry objects.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: ArrayList vs LinkedList in Java
description: Understand the differences between ArrayList and LinkedList and when to use each implementation.
content:
## ArrayList

ArrayList is backed by a dynamic array. It provides fast random access using indexes and is the preferred choice for most List operations.

## LinkedList

LinkedList stores elements as nodes connected through references. It can efficiently add or remove elements at the beginning or end of the list.

## Comparison

ArrayList provides O(1) access by index and generally better iteration performance. LinkedList requires traversal for index-based access but can perform insertions and deletions efficiently when a node reference is already available.

## Interview checkpoint

Explain internal data structures, memory consumption, resizing behavior, and the time complexities of common operations.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: HashMap Internal Working
description: Learn how HashMap stores data and provides efficient lookup performance.
content:
## Hashing mechanism

HashMap stores key-value pairs using buckets. The hashCode() method determines the bucket location, while equals() resolves collisions.

## Collision handling

Before Java 8, collisions were handled using linked lists. Since Java 8, buckets with many collisions can be converted into balanced trees for improved performance.

## Performance

Insertion, deletion, and retrieval operations typically run in O(1) time under good hash distribution.

## Interview checkpoint

Explain hashCode(), equals(), load factor, capacity, rehashing, bucket structure, and collision resolution techniques.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: HashSet vs TreeSet
description: Compare HashSet and TreeSet based on ordering, performance, and implementation.
content:
## HashSet

HashSet is implemented using HashMap internally. It does not maintain insertion order and offers fast lookup operations.

## TreeSet

TreeSet stores elements in sorted order using a Red-Black Tree implementation. Elements are automatically sorted based on natural ordering or a custom Comparator.

## Performance Comparison

HashSet operations generally run in O(1) time, while TreeSet operations run in O(log n) time.

## Interview checkpoint

Discuss ordering guarantees, null value handling, underlying data structures, and performance characteristics.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Comparable vs Comparator
description: Learn how object sorting works in Java collections.
content:
## Comparable

Comparable provides natural ordering for objects. The class implements the Comparable interface and overrides compareTo().

## Comparator

Comparator allows custom sorting logic without modifying the target class. Multiple sorting strategies can be implemented using different Comparator classes or lambda expressions.

## Use Cases

Use Comparable when there is a single natural ordering. Use Comparator when multiple sorting criteria are required.

## Interview checkpoint

Explain compareTo(), compare(), sorting collections, lambda-based comparators, and method references.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: ConcurrentHashMap for Thread-Safe Collections
description: Understand how ConcurrentHashMap supports high-performance concurrent access.
content:
## Why not HashMap?

HashMap is not thread-safe. Concurrent modifications by multiple threads may lead to inconsistent results.

## ConcurrentHashMap

ConcurrentHashMap allows multiple threads to perform read and write operations with better scalability than Hashtable or synchronized collections.

## Benefits

It minimizes locking and improves throughput in multithreaded environments.

## Interview checkpoint

Explain segment locking (pre-Java 8), bucket locking, thread safety, atomic operations, computeIfAbsent(), and concurrent performance advantages.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: HashMap String Key Equality Example
description: Understand how HashMap handles String keys using equals() and hashCode().
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: runAsync vs supplyAsync
description: Compare runAsync() and supplyAsync() methods in CompletableFuture.
content:
## runAsync()

runAsync() executes an asynchronous task without returning a result.

```java
CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> {
    System.out.println("Task Executed");
});
```

Returns:

```java
CompletableFuture<Void>
```

## supplyAsync()

supplyAsync() executes an asynchronous task and returns a value.

```java
CompletableFuture<String> future =
    CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> "Success");
```

Returns:

```java
CompletableFuture<T>
```

## Comparison

| Feature | runAsync() | supplyAsync() |
|----------|------------|--------------|
| Functional Interface | Runnable | Supplier<T> |
| Returns Result | No | Yes |
| Return Type | CompletableFuture<Void> | CompletableFuture<T> |
| Use Case | Fire and Forget | Compute and Return |

## Interview Checkpoint

Use runAsync() when no result is needed and supplyAsync() when the task produces a return value.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Native Library and JNI
description: Understand native code, native libraries, and the role of JNI.
content:
## What is Native Code?

Native code is code compiled specifically for an operating system or hardware platform such as Windows, Linux, x86, or ARM.

## Native Library

A native library usually contains C or C++ code.

Examples:

- DLL files on Windows.
- SO files on Linux.

## JNI (Java Native Interface)

JNI allows Java programs to interact with native libraries.

```java
public native void calculate();
```

The implementation is written in a native language such as C or C++.

## Interview Checkpoint

Using native libraries may impact Java's platform independence because native code is platform specific.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Can We Overload Varargs Methods?
description: Understand method overloading with variable arguments.
content:
## Answer

Yes, varargs methods can be overloaded.

## Example

```java
class Test {

    void test(String a1, String a2) {
        System.out.println("2 arguments");
    }

    void test(String... args) {
        System.out.println("Varargs");
    }
}
```

## Output

```java
test("A", "B")
```

Output:

```text
2 arguments
```

```java
test("A", "B", "C")
```

Output:

```text
Varargs
```

## Method Resolution

Java always prefers the most specific method.

## Interview Checkpoint

Varargs methods can be overloaded, but care should be taken to avoid ambiguous method calls.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Java exception handling and custom exceptions
description: Choose checked and unchecked exceptions appropriately and preserve useful error context.
content:
## Checked and unchecked exceptions

Checked exceptions must be declared or handled, while RuntimeException and its subclasses are unchecked. Use checked exceptions when callers can reasonably recover and are expected to account for the failure. Use unchecked exceptions for programming errors or failures that callers cannot meaningfully handle at that level.

## Preserve context

When translating an exception at an application boundary, keep the original cause so logs retain the underlying failure. Avoid catching broad exceptions only to return a success-shaped value or silently ignore the problem.

## Custom exceptions

Use a domain-specific exception when it makes an expected failure clearer to the caller, such as AccountNotFoundException. Keep exception names and messages useful, but do not place secrets or sensitive user data in messages that may be logged.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Parallel Stream in Java
description: Learn how Parallel Stream improves performance using multiple threads.
content:
## What is Parallel Stream?

Parallel Stream processes data using multiple threads from ForkJoinPool.

## Example

```java
list.parallelStream()
    .forEach(System.out::println);
```

## Advantages

- Faster processing for large datasets.
- Utilizes multicore processors.
- Simplifies concurrent programming.

## Disadvantages

- Overhead for small datasets.
- Order may not be preserved.
- Shared mutable state can cause issues.

## Interview Checkpoint

Use parallel streams only for CPU-intensive operations on sufficiently large datasets.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Function vs Predicate
description: Compare Function and Predicate functional interfaces.
content:
## Function<T,R>

Function accepts an input and returns a transformed result.

Method:

```java
R apply(T t)
```

Used with map().

## Predicate<T>

Predicate accepts input and returns a boolean value.

Method:

```java
boolean test(T t)
```

Used with filter().

## Comparison

| Feature | Function | Predicate |
|----------|----------|-----------|
| Input | Yes | Yes |
| Output | Any Type | Boolean |
| Method | apply() | test() |
| Stream Usage | map() | filter() |

## Interview Checkpoint

Predicate is mainly used for conditional checks whereas Function is used for data transformation.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Stream reduce() Method
description: Use reduce() for aggregation and accumulation operations.
content:
## What is reduce()?

The reduce() method performs a reduction operation on stream elements and returns a single result.

## Common Uses

- Sum
- Maximum
- Minimum
- Product
- Longest String

## Example

```java
Optional<String> longest = words.stream()
    .reduce((a,b) -> a.length() > b.length() ? a : b);
```

## Interview Checkpoint

reduce() combines multiple stream elements into a single result using an associative accumulation function.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Optional Class in Java 8
description: Learn how Optional helps prevent NullPointerException.
content:
## What is Optional?

Optional is a container object introduced in Java 8 to represent the presence or absence of a value.

## Why Use Optional?

It helps avoid NullPointerException and makes code more readable.

## Example

```java
Optional<String> name = Optional.of("Virendra");

name.ifPresent(System.out::println);
```

## Common Methods

- of()
- ofNullable()
- empty()
- isPresent()
- ifPresent()
- orElse()
- orElseGet()
- orElseThrow()

## Interview Checkpoint

Optional should be used as a return type when a value may be absent. Avoid using Optional for entity fields and method parameters.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Stateful vs Stateless Stream Operations
description: Learn the difference between stateful and stateless stream operations.
content:
## Stateless Operations

Stateless operations process each element independently.

Examples:

- map()
- filter()
- flatMap()
- peek()

### Characteristics

- No dependency on previous elements.
- Parallel processing friendly.
- Better performance.

## Stateful Operations

Stateful operations depend on other stream elements.

Examples:

- sorted()
- distinct()
- limit()
- skip()

### Characteristics

- Maintain state.
- Require additional memory.
- Less efficient in parallel processing.

## Interview Checkpoint

Stateless operations process elements independently, whereas stateful operations need information from other elements before producing results.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Intermediate vs Terminal Stream Operations
description: Understand how Stream pipelines are built and executed.
content:
## Intermediate Operations

Intermediate operations return another Stream.

Examples:

```java
map()
filter()
distinct()
sorted()
limit()
skip()
```

### Characteristics

- Lazy.
- Can be chained.
- No execution until terminal operation is invoked.

## Terminal Operations

Terminal operations produce the final result.

Examples:

```java
forEach()
collect()
count()
reduce()
findFirst()
min()
max()
```

### Characteristics

- Trigger stream execution.
- End the pipeline.

## Interview Checkpoint

Intermediate operations build the pipeline; terminal operations execute the pipeline and produce results.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: How JVM Works
description: Understand JVM architecture, class loading, execution, and memory management.
content:
## JVM Overview

The Java Virtual Machine (JVM) executes Java bytecode and provides platform independence.

## Execution Flow

1. Java source code (.java) is compiled into bytecode (.class) using javac.
2. ClassLoader loads required classes into memory.
3. Bytecode Verifier validates bytecode.
4. Execution Engine executes bytecode using Interpreter and JIT Compiler.
5. Garbage Collector manages memory automatically.

## Main Components

### Class Loader Subsystem

Loads classes dynamically into memory.

### Runtime Data Areas

- Method Area
- Heap Memory
- Java Stack
- PC Register
- Native Method Stack

### Execution Engine

Responsible for executing bytecode.

### Garbage Collector

Automatically removes unreachable objects.

## Interview Checkpoint

A JVM converts bytecode into machine-specific instructions using the interpreter and JIT compiler while managing memory and garbage collection automatically.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: How JVM Identifies Objects for Garbage Collection
description: Understand how the JVM determines whether an object is eligible for garbage collection.
content:
## Reachability Analysis

The JVM uses a process called Reachability Analysis to identify objects eligible for Garbage Collection.

The Garbage Collector starts from special references called GC Roots and checks whether an object can still be reached.

If an object cannot be reached from any GC Root, it becomes eligible for garbage collection.

## GC Roots

Common GC Roots include:

- Local variables in active stack frames.
- Static variables.
- Active threads.
- JNI (Native) references.

## Interview Checkpoint

Garbage Collection does not use reference counting. Modern JVMs use Reachability Analysis starting from GC Roots to determine whether an object is alive.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: MetaSpace vs PermGen
description: Understand the replacement of PermGen with MetaSpace in Java 8.
content:
## PermGen

- Available before Java 8.
- Fixed maximum size.
- Part of JVM heap memory.
- Frequent OutOfMemoryError issues.

## MetaSpace

- Introduced in Java 8.
- Uses native OS memory.
- Automatically grows when required.
- More efficient garbage collection.

## Comparison

| PermGen | MetaSpace |
|----------|-----------|
| Removed in Java 8 | Introduced in Java 8 |
| Fixed Size | Auto Expand |
| Heap Memory | Native Memory |
| Less Efficient | More Efficient |

## Interview Checkpoint

MetaSpace replaced PermGen in Java 8 and stores class metadata in native memory instead of heap memory.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: What is OutOfMemoryError?
description: Understand causes and types of OutOfMemoryError in Java.
content:
## Definition

OutOfMemoryError occurs when the JVM cannot allocate memory for new objects.

It is a subclass of VirtualMachineError.

## Common Causes

- Memory leak.
- Very large collections.
- Improper caching.
- Insufficient heap size.

## Common Types

### Java Heap Space

Occurs when heap memory is exhausted.

### Metaspace

Occurs when class metadata consumes excessive native memory.

### GC Overhead Limit Exceeded

Occurs when JVM spends too much time performing garbage collection without recovering meaningful memory.

## Interview Checkpoint

OutOfMemoryError is typically caused by insufficient memory allocation or application memory leaks.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Memory Leak in Java
description: Learn about memory leaks, detection methods, and troubleshooting techniques.
content:
## What is a Memory Leak?

A memory leak occurs when objects are no longer needed but are still reachable, preventing garbage collection.

## Common Causes

- Static collections.
- Unclosed resources.
- Event listeners.
- Caching objects indefinitely.

## Detection Techniques

### Heap Dump Analysis

Heap dumps capture snapshots of all objects currently in memory.

### Memory Analyzer Tool (MAT)

Used to identify retained objects and memory leaks.

### JVM Profilers

- VisualVM
- JProfiler
- YourKit

## Interview Checkpoint

Memory leaks are caused by unintended object retention, not by JVM garbage collectors failing to work.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: How to Solve Java Heap Space Error
description: Common approaches to troubleshoot and fix heap space issues.
content:
## Problem

```text
java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
```

## Solution 1: Increase Heap Size

```bash
-Xms1024m
-Xmx1024m
```

Where:

- Xms = Initial Heap Size
- Xmx = Maximum Heap Size

## Solution 2: Identify Memory Leaks

Analyze:

- Heap Dumps
- Eclipse MAT
- VisualVM
- JProfiler

## Solution 3: Optimize Collections

Avoid keeping unnecessary objects in memory.

## Interview Checkpoint

Increasing heap memory may solve the symptom, but memory leak analysis is required to solve the root cause.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: ClassNotFoundException vs NoClassDefFoundError
description: Understand the difference between runtime class loading problems.
content:
## ClassNotFoundException

Occurs when a class is explicitly loaded using:

```java
Class.forName()
```

or

```java
ClassLoader.loadClass()
```

and the class is not found in the classpath.

## NoClassDefFoundError

Occurs when a class was available during compilation but not found at runtime.

## Comparison

| Feature | ClassNotFoundException | NoClassDefFoundError |
|----------|----------------------|---------------------|
| Type | Exception | Error |
| Cause | Class not found during explicit loading | Class missing at runtime |
| Recoverable | Yes | Usually No |

## Interview Checkpoint

ClassNotFoundException occurs while loading a class explicitly. NoClassDefFoundError occurs when JVM expects a class that existed at compile time but is missing during execution.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Java Concurrency and Thread Safety
description: Learn thread creation, synchronization, and common concurrency utilities used in enterprise applications.
content:
## Understanding threads

A thread is the smallest unit of execution within a Java process. Multiple threads can execute concurrently, allowing applications to perform background processing without blocking the main workflow.

## Thread safety

When multiple threads access shared data, race conditions can occur. Synchronization, locks, atomic variables, and concurrent collections help protect shared resources.

## Interview checkpoint

Be prepared to explain synchronized, volatile, ReentrantLock, AtomicInteger, and the difference between ConcurrentHashMap and HashMap.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Callable vs Runnable
description: Understand the differences between Callable and Runnable interfaces.
content:
## Runnable

Runnable is a functional interface used to execute a task in a separate thread.

```java
Runnable task = () -> {
    System.out.println("Running task");
};
```

### Characteristics

- Does not return a result.
- Cannot throw checked exceptions.
- Can be executed using Thread or ExecutorService.

## Callable

Callable is a functional interface introduced in Java 5.

```java
Callable<String> task = () -> "Success";
```

### Characteristics

- Returns a result.
- Can throw checked exceptions.
- Executed using ExecutorService.
- Returns Future object.

## Comparison

| Feature | Runnable | Callable |
|----------|----------|----------|
| Return Value | No | Yes |
| Checked Exception | No | Yes |
| Method | run() | call() |
| Return Type | void | Generic Type |

## Interview Checkpoint

Use Runnable when no result is needed. Use Callable when a task must return data or throw checked exceptions.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: What is CompletableFuture?
content:
## What is CompletableFuture?

CompletableFuture was introduced in Java 8 to support asynchronous and non-blocking programming.

It belongs to:

```java
java.util.concurrent
```

## Advantages

- Non-blocking execution.
- Supports callback chaining.
- Better exception handling.
- Combines multiple asynchronous tasks.

## Example

```java
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> "Java")
    .thenApply(String::toUpperCase)
    .thenAccept(System.out::println);
```

## Common Methods

- supplyAsync()
- runAsync()
- thenApply()
- thenAccept()
- thenCombine()
- exceptionally()
- join()

## Interview Checkpoint

CompletableFuture extends Future and solves many limitations such as chaining, combining tasks, and exception handling.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Future vs CompletableFuture
content:
## Future

Future represents the result of an asynchronous computation.

### Limitations

- No chaining support.
- No combining of multiple futures.
- Limited exception handling.
- Blocking get() method.

## CompletableFuture

CompletableFuture extends Future and supports asynchronous pipelines.

### Advantages

- Chaining operations.
- Combining multiple tasks.
- Better exception handling.
- Non-blocking execution.

## Comparison

| Feature | Future | CompletableFuture |
|----------|--------|------------------|
| Chaining | No | Yes |
| Combine Tasks | No | Yes |
| Exception Handling | Limited | Advanced |
| Async Pipeline | No | Yes |

## Interview Checkpoint

CompletableFuture is the preferred modern approach for asynchronous programming because it supports chaining, composition, and exception handling.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: ExecutorService submit() vs execute()
description: Compare execute() and submit() methods of ExecutorService.
content:
## execute()

The execute() method accepts a Runnable task and returns nothing.

```java
executor.execute(() -> System.out.println("Task"));
```

Return Type:

```java
void
```

## submit()

The submit() method accepts Runnable or Callable and returns a Future.

```java
Future<String> future = executor.submit(() -> "Success");
```

## Comparison

| Feature | execute() | submit() |
|----------|-----------|----------|
| Return Value | No | Future |
| Runnable Support | Yes | Yes |
| Callable Support | No | Yes |
| Result Retrieval | No | Yes |

## Interview Checkpoint

Use execute() when no result is required. Use submit() when task status or return value is needed.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Abstract Class vs Interface
description: Understand the differences, use cases, and interview expectations around Abstract Classes and Interfaces.
content:
## Abstract Class

An abstract class can contain both abstract and concrete methods. It can have constructors, instance variables, static members, and method implementations. It is used when related classes share common state or behavior.

## Interface

An interface defines a contract that implementing classes must follow. Since Java 8, interfaces can contain default and static methods. Since Java 9, interfaces can also contain private methods.

## Key Differences

- Abstract class supports constructors.
- Interface supports multiple inheritance.
- Abstract class can contain state.
- Interface focuses on behavior.
- A class can extend only one abstract class but implement multiple interfaces.

## Interview Checkpoint

Use an abstract class when multiple related classes share common logic. Use an interface when different classes need to provide the same behavior contract.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Class vs Interface
description: Learn the purpose and differences between Class and Interface in Java.
content:
## Class

A class is a blueprint for creating objects. It contains fields, methods, constructors, and business logic. Objects are created from classes.

## Interface

An interface is a contract that defines what a class should do. It contains method declarations and supports abstraction.

## Key Differences

- Class can contain implementation and state.
- Interface defines behavior.
- Classes support single inheritance.
- Interfaces support multiple inheritance.

## Interview Checkpoint

Explain that a class represents an object while an interface represents a capability or contract.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: String vs StringBuffer vs StringBuilder
description: Compare mutability, thread safety, and performance of String, StringBuffer, and StringBuilder.
content:
## String

String is immutable. Every modification creates a new object. String literals are stored in the String Constant Pool.

## StringBuffer

StringBuffer is mutable and thread-safe because its methods are synchronized.

## StringBuilder

StringBuilder is mutable but not thread-safe. It provides better performance than StringBuffer.

## Performance

StringBuilder > StringBuffer > String (for multiple concatenations).

## Interview Checkpoint

Use String for constants, StringBuilder for single-threaded string manipulation, and StringBuffer for multithreaded string manipulation.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: What is an Immutable Class?
description: Understand immutable objects and why they are important in Java.
content:
## Definition

An immutable class is a class whose state cannot be changed after object creation.

## Example

String is the most common immutable class in Java.

## Characteristics

- State never changes after creation.
- Thread-safe by design.
- Suitable for caching and HashMap keys.

## Benefits

- Improved thread safety.
- Easier debugging.
- Predictable behavior.

## Interview Checkpoint

Mention String, wrapper classes, LocalDate, and LocalDateTime as common immutable classes.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: How to Create an Immutable Class
description: Steps and best practices to create an immutable class in Java.
content:
## Rules

1. Make the class final.
2. Make all fields private and final.
3. Initialize fields only through constructor.
4. Do not provide setters.
5. Return defensive copies for mutable objects.
6. Create defensive copies inside constructor.

## Mutable Object Handling

If the class contains mutable objects such as Date, create copies instead of storing external references.

## Interview Checkpoint

The most important interview point is defensive copying of mutable fields like Date to preserve immutability.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Four Pillars of OOPS
description: Learn the fundamental object-oriented principles of Java.
content:
## Encapsulation

Binding data and methods together while restricting direct access using private access modifiers.

## Inheritance

Acquiring properties and behavior from another class to improve code reusability.

## Polymorphism

One interface, multiple implementations. Achieved through method overloading and method overriding.

## Abstraction

Hiding implementation details while exposing only essential functionality using abstract classes and interfaces.

## Interview Checkpoint

Explain each pillar with practical examples from real-world projects.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Shallow Cloning vs Deep Cloning
description: Understand the differences between shallow copy and deep copy, common interview scenarios, and practical use cases.
content:
## Shallow Cloning

Shallow cloning creates a new object but copies references of nested objects instead of creating independent copies. Changes made to referenced child objects are visible in both original and cloned objects.

Object.clone() performs shallow copy by default.

### Example

If an Employee object contains an Address object, a shallow clone will create a new Employee object but both Employee objects will point to the same Address instance.

## Deep Cloning

Deep cloning creates a completely independent copy of the object including all referenced child objects. Changes in the cloned object's nested objects do not affect the original object.

### Example

If an Employee object contains an Address object, deep cloning creates both a new Employee object and a new Address object.

## Real-Life Example

Think of a house:

- Shallow Clone: Two people have different keys for the same house.
- Deep Clone: A completely new house is built with its own key.

## Comparison

| Feature | Shallow Clone | Deep Clone |
|----------|--------------|-------------|
| Main Object | Copied | Copied |
| Child Objects | Shared References | Independent Copies |
| Memory Usage | Lower | Higher |
| Performance | Faster | Slower |
| Object Independence | No | Yes |

## Interview Checkpoint

Object.clone() performs shallow copy by default. Deep copy requires manually copying all referenced objects or using serialization-based cloning techniques. Shallow Copy = Shared References. Deep Copy = Independent References.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Best Choice for String Concatenation
description: Learn when to use String, StringBuffer, and StringBuilder for string concatenation.
content:
## String

String is immutable. Every concatenation operation creates a new String object. Excessive concatenation leads to memory overhead and performance degradation.

## StringBuffer

StringBuffer is mutable and thread-safe because all modification methods are synchronized. It is suitable for multithreaded environments.

## StringBuilder

StringBuilder is mutable and not synchronized. Since it avoids synchronization overhead, it provides better performance than StringBuffer.

## Performance Ranking

StringBuilder > StringBuffer > String

for repeated concatenation operations.

## When to Use

- Use String for constant and read-only values.
- Use StringBuilder in single-threaded applications.
- Use StringBuffer in multi-threaded applications where thread safety is required.

## Interview Checkpoint

For repeated string concatenation, StringBuilder is the most efficient choice. String should not be used in loops that perform frequent concatenation.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Can We Extend String Class?
description: Understand why String cannot be inherited in Java.
content:
## Answer

No, we cannot extend the String class.

## Reason

The String class is declared as final.

```java
public final class String
```

Because it is final, inheritance is not allowed.

## Why String is Final

- Security
- Performance optimization
- Immutability guarantee
- String Pool consistency

## Interview Checkpoint

String is final to preserve immutability. If inheritance were allowed, subclasses could break String behavior and compromise security.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Method Visibility Rules in Overriding
description: Learn how method visibility works during method overriding.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Main Method in Parent and Child Classes
description: Understand how main() behaves in inheritance.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Cohesion in Java
description: Understand high cohesion and why it is important for maintainable code.
content:
## What is Cohesion?

Cohesion measures how closely related the responsibilities of a class are.

## High Cohesion

A class focuses on a single responsibility.

Benefits:

- Easier maintenance.
- Better readability.
- Improved reusability.
- Easier testing.

## Low Cohesion Example

A class that performs mathematical calculations and displays UI windows.

## High Cohesion Example

```java
class Calculator {}
class Display {}
```

Each class has a single responsibility.

## Interview Checkpoint

High Cohesion means a class performs one well-defined task. High cohesion and low coupling are considered good design principles.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Marker Interface in Java
description: Learn what marker interfaces are and their purpose in Java.
content:
## What is a Marker Interface?

A marker interface is an interface that contains no methods or fields.

It is used to provide metadata to the JVM or a framework.

## Examples

```java
Serializable
Cloneable
Remote
```

## Example

```java
public interface Serializable {
}
```

## Purpose

The interface acts as a marker indicating special behavior.

## Interview Checkpoint

Marker interfaces communicate capabilities to the JVM or framework without requiring method implementation.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Why Can Abstract Classes Have Constructors?
description: Understand why abstract classes can define constructors and how they are used.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Why Use SerialVersionUID?
description: Understand the role of SerialVersionUID during serialization and deserialization.
content:
## Purpose

SerialVersionUID ensures that the same class version is used during serialization and deserialization.

## Example

```java
private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;
```

## Custom SerialVersionUID

- Defined by developer.
- Stable across versions.
- Recommended for production.

## JVM Generated SerialVersionUID

- Generated automatically.
- Changes when class structure changes.
- May break backward compatibility.

## Interview Checkpoint

Always define SerialVersionUID explicitly in serializable classes to avoid InvalidClassException.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Vertical Scaling vs Horizontal Scaling
description: Compare scale-up and scale-out approaches used in enterprise systems.
content:
## Vertical Scaling (Scale Up)

Vertical scaling increases resources on the same machine.

Examples:

- More CPU
- More RAM
- Faster SSD

## Horizontal Scaling (Scale Out)

Horizontal scaling adds additional servers or machines.

Examples:

- Multiple application servers
- Load balancing across nodes
- Distributed systems

## Comparison

| Feature | Vertical Scaling | Horizontal Scaling |
|----------|------------------|--------------------|
| Resources | Increase server power | Add servers |
| Cost | High | Flexible |
| Availability | Lower | Higher |
| Scalability | Limited | Almost unlimited |

## Interview Checkpoint

Modern microservices architectures prefer horizontal scaling because it increases availability and fault tolerance.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Kafka Consumer Offset Management
description: Understand Kafka offsets, commits, and message consumption strategies.
content:
## What is an offset?

An offset represents the position of a record within a Kafka partition. Consumers use offsets to track processed messages.

## Auto and manual commits

Auto commits simplify implementation but may lead to duplicate processing. Manual commits provide better control and reliability.

## Interview checkpoint

Explain auto.offset.reset, earliest vs latest, consumer groups, offset commit strategies, and rebalancing.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Managing application configuration with Kubernetes ConfigMaps
description: Separate non-sensitive configuration from container images and understand update behavior.
content:
## Store non-sensitive settings

A ConfigMap stores non-confidential key-value configuration separately from an application image. Pods can consume its values as environment variables, command arguments, or mounted files.

## Understand when changes take effect

Environment variables are set when a container starts, so changing a ConfigMap does not update a running process's environment. Mounted ConfigMap files may update eventually, but the application must be able to reload them. A rollout restart is a common way to ensure Pods use updated configuration.

## Keep secrets separate

Do not put credentials or tokens in a ConfigMap. Use a Secret with appropriate access controls, and remember that default base64 encoding is not encryption.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Kubernetes readiness and liveness probes
description: Learn how probes help Kubernetes route traffic and recover unhealthy containers.
content:
## Readiness

A readiness probe indicates whether a container is ready to receive traffic. When it fails, Kubernetes removes the Pod from matching Service endpoints while leaving the container running.

## Liveness

A liveness probe detects a container that cannot make progress. Repeated failures cause the container to restart. Avoid making a liveness check depend on a temporary external service, which could trigger unnecessary restart loops.

## Startup probes

A startup probe gives slow-starting applications time to initialize before liveness and readiness checks begin. Configure thresholds and periods based on real application startup behavior.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Designing clear service boundaries in microservices
description: Use business capabilities and data ownership to define services that can evolve independently.
content:
## Start with business capabilities

A service boundary should reflect a cohesive business capability, not simply a technical layer or database table. Group behavior and the data it owns together so the service can enforce its rules consistently.

## Make ownership explicit

Each service should be the source of truth for its data. Other services interact through stable APIs or events rather than directly changing its database. This reduces hidden coupling and allows internal schemas to evolve.

## Avoid premature splitting

A distributed boundary adds network failures, operational overhead, and consistency challenges. Start with a modular design and split a service when independent scaling, deployment, ownership, or fault isolation provides a concrete benefit.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Circuit Breaker Pattern in Microservices
description: Prevent cascading failures by isolating failing services using circuit breakers.
content:
## Purpose

A circuit breaker prevents repeated requests to an unavailable service, reducing resource consumption and improving system stability.

## States

The circuit breaker operates in Closed, Open, and Half-Open states. Requests are blocked when the circuit is Open.

## Interview checkpoint

Be ready to explain Resilience4j, fallback methods, retry patterns, timeout configuration, and bulkhead isolation.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Using MySQL joins and aggregation safely
description: Combine related rows, group results, and avoid common aggregate-query mistakes.
content:
## Join related data

An INNER JOIN returns rows that match in both inputs. A LEFT JOIN preserves every row from the left input and returns nulls for missing right-side matches. Put conditions in ON when they define a match; a filter on the right-side table in WHERE may remove null-extended rows and effectively change a LEFT JOIN into an inner filter.

## Group and aggregate

GROUP BY produces one result per group, and aggregate functions such as COUNT and SUM calculate values for each group. Use HAVING to filter groups after aggregation; use WHERE to filter input rows before grouping.

## Verify query behavior

Check whether joins multiply rows before summing values, add indexes to frequently joined or filtered columns where appropriate, and inspect the execution plan with EXPLAIN.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Oracle analytic functions for ranking and running totals
description: Use analytic functions to calculate rankings and aggregates without collapsing result rows.
content:
## Analytic function structure

An analytic function uses an OVER clause with optional PARTITION BY and ORDER BY clauses. Unlike GROUP BY, it can calculate a value across a set of related rows while keeping each input row in the output.

## Ranking examples

ROW_NUMBER assigns a unique sequence within each partition. RANK gives ties the same rank and leaves gaps afterward, while DENSE_RANK gives ties the same rank without gaps. Use a deterministic tie-breaker in ORDER BY when the result must be repeatable.

## Running totals

SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY transaction_time, id) can calculate a running total for each account. Choose the window frame intentionally, especially when rows share the same ordering value.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Reading PostgreSQL query plans with EXPLAIN
description: Use query plans and measured row counts to investigate slow PostgreSQL queries.
content:
## Inspect the plan

EXPLAIN shows the plan PostgreSQL expects to use, including scans, joins, estimated costs, and estimated row counts. EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement and reports actual timing and row counts, which can reveal where estimates differ from reality.

## Compare estimates and actuals

Large differences may indicate stale statistics, correlated data, or a query shape the planner cannot estimate well. Review the most expensive nodes and the number of rows processed rather than assuming an index scan is always faster than a sequential scan.

## Use care with write statements

EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the query. For a statement that changes data, test in a safe transaction or on representative non-production data and roll back when appropriate.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Managing subscriptions and cleanup with React useEffect
description: Synchronize a component with external systems and clean up before effects are replaced.
content:
## Effects and synchronization

useEffect is intended for synchronizing a component with an external system, such as a browser event listener, timer, or network connection. It is not required for every calculation that can be derived directly while rendering.

## Return a cleanup function

An effect can return a cleanup function to remove listeners, clear timers, or cancel supported work. React runs cleanup before the effect is set up again with changed dependencies and when the component unmounts.

## Keep dependencies accurate

Include reactive values used by the effect. Missing dependencies can cause stale values, while unstable objects or functions can cause repeated runs. Simplify the effect or stabilize the inputs when repeated setup is not intended.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Spring Bean Lifecycle Explained
description: Understand how Spring creates, manages, and destroys beans within the application context.
content:
## Bean creation

Spring creates beans when the application context starts. Dependencies are injected before initialization methods are executed.

## Bean lifecycle stages

Instantiation, dependency injection, initialization, usage, and destruction are the major stages of the bean lifecycle.

## Interview checkpoint

Explain @PostConstruct, @PreDestroy, BeanPostProcessor, singleton scope, and prototype scope.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Building REST endpoints with Spring Boot
description: Review controller responsibilities, request mapping, validation, and response status codes.
content:
## Controller fundamentals

A Spring MVC controller maps HTTP requests to application behavior. Use @RestController for JSON APIs and map resources with annotations such as @GetMapping and @PostMapping.

## Keep responsibilities clear

Controllers should validate request shape, delegate business rules to a service, and return suitable HTTP responses. Use request DTOs rather than binding persistence entities directly. Add Bean Validation constraints and handle errors consistently.

## Interview checkpoint

Be ready to explain why POST creates a resource, why PUT replaces a resource, and when PATCH is appropriate. Return 201 Created for a successful creation and include a Location header when practical.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Spring Security: authentication and request authorization
description: Separate authentication from authorization and apply least-privilege access to Spring APIs.
content:
## Authentication versus authorization

Authentication establishes who is making a request. Authorization decides whether that identity may perform a particular action on a resource. A valid login alone should not grant every application permission.

## Protect request routes

Configure security rules so public endpoints are explicitly identified and protected routes require an authenticated principal and the appropriate authority. Prefer denying access by default over leaving new endpoints unintentionally public.

## Check access at the resource boundary

For sensitive operations, enforce authorization on the server and consider method-level checks for business actions. Client-side route guards and hidden controls improve user experience but are not a security boundary. Test both unauthenticated and insufficiently privileged requests.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: What is Angular and Why is it Used?
description: Understand Angular fundamentals and its use in modern web development.
content:
## What is Angular?

Angular is a TypeScript-based open-source frontend framework developed by Google for building dynamic Single Page Applications (SPA).

## Why Use Angular?

- Component-based architecture.
- Two-way data binding.
- Dependency Injection support.
- Routing support.
- Lazy loading support.
- Built-in form handling.
- Powerful CLI.

## Common Use Cases

- Enterprise applications.
- Admin dashboards.
- E-commerce applications.
- CRM and ERP systems.

## Interview Checkpoint

Angular is a complete frontend framework that provides routing, dependency injection, forms, state management integration, and UI component development capabilities.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Lazy Loading vs Eager Loading in Angular
description: Learn the difference between lazy loading and eager loading modules.
content:
## Eager Loading

All modules are loaded during application startup.

### Advantages

- Simple configuration.
- No delay after navigation.

### Disadvantages

- Larger bundle size.
- Slower initial application load.

## Lazy Loading

Modules are loaded only when required.

```typescript
{
  path: 'admin',
  loadChildren: () => import('./admin/admin.module')
    .then(m => m.AdminModule)
}
```

### Advantages

- Faster initial loading.
- Smaller bundle size.
- Better performance.

## Interview Checkpoint

Lazy loading improves application startup performance by loading feature modules only when users navigate to them.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Constructor vs ngOnInit
description: Understand the differences between constructor and ngOnInit lifecycle hook.
content:
## Constructor

The constructor is executed when the component class is instantiated.

Used for:

- Dependency Injection.
- Basic object initialization.

```typescript
constructor(private service: UserService) {}
```

## ngOnInit

ngOnInit is a lifecycle hook called after Angular initializes component properties.

```typescript
ngOnInit(): void {
  this.loadUsers();
}
```

Used for:

- API calls.
- Business initialization logic.
- Component setup.

## Can We Call ngOnInit() From Constructor?

Technically yes, but it is not recommended. Angular automatically invokes ngOnInit at the proper lifecycle stage.

## Interview Checkpoint

Constructor is for Dependency Injection. ngOnInit is for initialization logic after Angular creates the component.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: One-Way Binding vs Two-Way Binding
content: ## One-Way Binding Data flows in a single direction. ### Interpolation ```html {{name}} ``` ### Property Binding ```html ``` ## Two-Way Binding Data flows in both directions. ```html ``` When the value changes in UI, component data updates automatically. ## Interview Checkpoint Two-way binding is achieved using ngModel and combines property binding with event binding.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Observable vs Promise
description: Compare Observables and Promises used in Angular applications.
content:
## Promise

A Promise returns a single value asynchronously.

```typescript
promise.then(data => console.log(data));
```

## Observable

An Observable can emit multiple values over time.

```typescript
observable.subscribe(data => console.log(data));
```

## Comparison

| Feature | Promise | Observable |
|----------|----------|------------|
| Values | One | Multiple |
| Cancellation | No | Yes |
| Lazy Execution | No | Yes |
| Operators | Limited | Rich RxJS Operators |

## Interview Checkpoint

Angular HttpClient returns Observables because they support cancellation, transformation, and multiple emissions.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: What is Router Outlet?
description: Understand the purpose of router-outlet in Angular routing.
content:
## What is Router Outlet?

Router outlet is a directive that acts as a placeholder for routed components.

```html
<router-outlet></router-outlet>
```

When navigation occurs, Angular loads the corresponding component inside the router outlet.

## Example

```typescript
{ path: 'users', component: UserComponent }
```

Navigating to /users loads UserComponent inside router-outlet.

## Interview Checkpoint

router-outlet serves as the container where Angular dynamically displays routed components.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: What are Directives in Angular?
description: Learn the types of Angular directives and their usage.
content:
## What is a Directive?

A Directive is used to modify the behavior or appearance of DOM elements.

## Types of Directives

### Component Directive

Components are directives with templates.

### Structural Directives

Change DOM layout.

Examples:

```html
*ngIf
*ngFor
*ngSwitch
```

### Attribute Directives

Change element appearance or behavior.

Examples:

```html
ngClass
ngStyle
```

## Interview Checkpoint

Structural directives add or remove DOM elements, whereas attribute directives modify existing elements.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Router, Component and Module
content:
## Component

A component controls a view.

```typescript
@Component({...})
export class UserComponent {}
```

## Module

A module groups related components, services, pipes, and directives.

```typescript
@NgModule({...})
export class AppModule {}
```

## Router

The Angular Router enables navigation between application views.

```typescript
RouterModule.forRoot(routes)
```

## Interview Checkpoint

Modules organize the application, components represent UI, and the router handles navigation.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Pipes in Angular
description: Transform data for display using Angular Pipes.
content:
## What is a Pipe?

Pipes transform data before it is displayed in the view.

## Built-in Pipes

- date
- currency
- uppercase
- lowercase
- percent
- json

## Example

```html
{{ today | date }}
{{ amount | currency }}
```

## Custom Pipe

```typescript
@Pipe({ name: 'capitalize' })
```

## Interview Checkpoint

Pipes are used only for presentation-layer transformations and should not contain business logic.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Dependency Injection in Angular
description: Understand Angular Dependency Injection and service management.
content:
## What is Dependency Injection?

Dependency Injection (DI) is the process of supplying required dependencies to a class rather than creating them manually.

## Example

```typescript
constructor(private userService: UserService) {}
```

Angular automatically creates and injects the service.

## Benefits

- Loose coupling.
- Better testability.
- Reusability.
- Maintainability.

## Interview Checkpoint

Angular uses a hierarchical injector system to manage service instances throughout the application.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Singleton Service in Angular
description: Single instance service across the application.
content: A singleton service has only one instance throughout the application. It is commonly created using providedIn:'root' and is used for shared business logic and application-wide state.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: What is RxJS?
content: RxJS is a library for asynchronous and event-based programming using Observables. Angular uses RxJS for HTTP requests, routing events, and real-time data streams.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Attribute Directive vs Structural Directive
content: Structural directives modify the DOM layout (e.g., *ngIf, *ngFor). Attribute directives modify the appearance or behavior of existing elements (e.g., ngClass, ngStyle).
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: What is Module?
content: A module is a container that groups components, services, directives, and pipes into a logical unit. Example: AppModule, FeatureModule.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Component vs Service vs Module
content: Component handles UI, Service contains business logic, and Module organizes related Angular artifacts.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: What is Node.js?
content: Node.js is a JavaScript runtime built on Chrome V8. It is required for Angular CLI, npm, and project builds.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: @Component Decorator
description: Marks a class as Angular Component.
content: @Component is a decorator that defines metadata such as selector, template, and styles for a component.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: What is Change Detection?
content: Change Detection automatically updates the view whenever component data changes. Angular supports Default and OnPush strategies.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: jQuery map() vs remove()
content: map() transforms selected elements into a collection. remove() deletes elements from the DOM.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: document.ready()
content: document.ready() executes JavaScript code after the DOM is fully loaded.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: jQuery Chaining
content: jQuery chaining allows multiple methods to be executed on the same element in a single statement.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: IndexedDB
content: IndexedDB is a browser-based NoSQL database used to store large amounts of structured data for offline and high-performance applications.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Spring Cloud Config Server
content: Spring Cloud Config Server provides centralized externalized configuration for distributed microservices. It is enabled using @EnableConfigServer.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Netflix Eureka Server
content: Eureka is a service registry where microservices register and discover each other dynamically. Annotations: @EnableEurekaServer and @EnableEurekaClient.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Hystrix Circuit Breaker
content: Hystrix provides fault tolerance using the Circuit Breaker pattern. It stops sending requests to failing services and helps prevent system-wide failures.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: API Gateway Pattern
content: API Gateway acts as a centralized entry point that handles routing, security, load balancing, and request aggregation for multiple microservices.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Why Use API Gateway?
content: API Gateway avoids hardcoded URLs, centralizes security, simplifies routing, supports load balancing, and prevents frontend changes when backend services change.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Netflix Ribbon
content: Ribbon provides client-side load balancing using algorithms such as Round Robin. It supports fault tolerance, caching, and multiple communication protocols.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Zipkin Distributed Tracing
content: Zipkin is a distributed tracing system used to monitor and visualize requests flowing through multiple microservices.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Common Spring Cloud Ports
content: Config Server: 8888, Eureka Server: 8761, API Gateway: 8765, Zipkin: 9411.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: What is Jenkins?
content: Jenkins is an open-source automation server used for Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery (CI/CD). It automates build, test, and deployment processes.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: POLL SCM in Jenkins
content: POLL SCM periodically checks the source repository for changes and automatically triggers a build if changes are detected.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Jenkins Cron Schedule
content: Jenkins uses cron expressions. Example: */5 * * * * runs every 5 minutes. 0 8 * * * runs daily at 8:00 AM.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Saga Pattern
content: Saga manages distributed transactions through a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions if a step fails.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Saga Choreography
content: In choreography, services communicate through events without a central coordinator. Each service reacts to events and triggers the next step.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Saga Orchestration
content: In orchestration, a central orchestrator coordinates service execution and manages rollback actions when failures occur.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: What is Resilience4j?
content: Resilience4j is a lightweight fault-tolerance library that provides Circuit Breaker, Retry, Rate Limiter, Bulkhead, Time Limiter, and Cache patterns.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Circuit Breaker in Resilience4j
content: Circuit Breaker stops requests to failing services and quickly returns fallback responses until the service recovers.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Rate Limiter
content: Rate Limiter restricts the number of requests allowed within a specific period to protect services from overload.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Retry Mechanism
content: Retry automatically re-executes failed operations a configured number of times before reporting failure.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Bulkhead Pattern
content: Bulkhead limits concurrent requests to prevent one failing service from consuming all system resources.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: Spring Cloud Stream
content: Spring Cloud Stream simplifies building event-driven microservices using messaging systems such as Kafka and RabbitMQ.
author: Tech Interview Hub

title: @EnableEurekaClient vs @EnableDiscoveryClient
content: @EnableEurekaClient works only with Eureka. @EnableDiscoveryClient is registry-independent and supports Eureka, Consul, and Zookeeper.
author: Tech Interview Hub
